title: Meta Faces Landmark Social Media Trial as States Seek $1.4 Trillion in Child Addiction Damages
excerpt: Opening arguments begin Tuesday in Oakland as 29 state attorneys general accuse the tech giant of engineering Facebook and Instagram to addict children.
body:
• Twenty-nine state attorneys general are taking Meta to trial in Oakland, alleging the company illegally collected children's data and designed addictive platforms.
  • Four states — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — are seeking up to $1.4 trillion in penalties, nearly matching Meta's $1.5 trillion market cap.
  • The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Meta's bid to delay the trial, ruling that Section 230 offers a "defense against liability," not immunity from suit.
  • Meta has already spent $2.4 billion on litigation in a single quarter and was ordered to pay $567 million by a New Mexico court.

Opening arguments begin Tuesday in what may be the most consequential legal challenge in Meta's history. U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will preside over a six-week trial in Oakland, California, where 29 state attorneys general allege the company engineered Facebook and Instagram to addict young users and illegally harvested their data.

The Stakes: $1.4 Trillion and Counting

Meta has disclosed that four of the plaintiffs — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — are seeking penalties that could total $1.4 trillion, according to a court filing reported by Reuters. The figure approaches the company's roughly $1.5 trillion market capitalization. Meta has called such a sanction one with "no analog in the history of consumer protection enforcement."

https://x.com/ThePatriotOasis/status/2089377798141972906

The states' penalty calculations, which remain sealed, are based on multiplying the number of violations by fine amounts set by state consumer protection laws. The number of violations is derived from the estimated number of young users affected by Meta's platforms.

"A trial is how the public finds out what Meta knew about its products' impact on children, when it knew it, and what it chose to do with that knowledge. Meta has fought to keep that evidence from the public."

— Attorneys for the state plaintiffs

Advisory Jury and a Shifting Legal Strategy

In an unusual procedural twist, Rogers has impaneled an advisory jury of five women and three men — a panel whose verdict will not be binding. The judge selected them during a five-hour session on August 12, noting that an advisory jury was "prudent" because the issues at stake "impact the daily lives of millions of social media users."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=2KdT7j62fRU

Meta originally demanded a jury trial when the state attorneys general filed suit in 2023 but reversed course in March, requesting a bench trial instead. That pivot came as juries in both New Mexico and Los Angeles delivered verdicts against the company in separate social media addiction cases. Rogers denied Meta's request and seated the advisory panel over the company's objections.

During jury selection, nearly all prospective jurors agreed that teens face a mental health crisis and that social media bears at least some responsibility. When a Colorado prosecutor asked for a show of hands on whether parents alone were responsible for children's social media problems, only two of roughly 50 people agreed. Neither was selected for the jury.

A Mounting Legal Bill

The trial comes amid a cascade of legal setbacks for Meta. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last week rejected the company's attempt to invoke Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act to block the lawsuits, ruling that the statute offers a "defense against liability" rather than blanket immunity from being sued. That decision also cleared the path for more than 3,000 additional social media addiction lawsuits brought by individuals and school districts against Meta, Google, Snap, and ByteDance.

Meta spent $2.4 billion on litigation in the most recent quarter alone, according to its latest earnings report, with the bulk related to youth social media addiction claims. A New Mexico court also ordered the company to pay $567 million into a teenage mental health fund, on top of a prior fine in the same case. In March, juries in both California and New Mexico ruled against Meta in bellwether social media addiction cases — including the first-ever trial of its kind, where a jury voted 10-2 to hold Meta and Google liable for a young woman's social media addiction.

What It Means for Big Tech

The trial is being watched closely across Silicon Valley, where other platform operators face similar legal exposure. A school district trial against multiple tech companies is set for February. Legal experts say defeats for Meta could spur settlement negotiations akin to the deals that tarnished the tobacco and opioid industries.

A Meta spokesperson said the company stands by its "record of creating strong protections for teens." The California Attorney General's office said the plaintiffs are "pleased to be proceeding toward trial on our claims." Rogers, who previously presided over an advisory-jury trial involving Elon Musk and OpenAI in May, will have the final word.
